summary: An informational memo proposing a new naming plan for directory-enabled applications, noting that the usual X.500 naming approach has been an obstacle to wide deployment. It builds on strengths of widely used naming systems.

plainLanguage.summary: A simpler way to name people and things in a directory so ordinary programs can use it.

questions: what is the dc attribute in ldap
how are ldap names built from domain names
why was x.500 naming hard to deploy
subtitle: A plan for naming directory entries by reusing DNS domain names and e-mail style identifiers instead of X.500 registrations.

tldr.problem: The conventional X.500 way of naming directory entries needed organization-name registrations that barely exist, and common names collide, so directory-enabled applications struggled to spread on the Internet.
tldr.mechanism: Build the upper part of a directory name from the labels of a registered DNS name using the dc attribute, and name leaf objects with uid (reusing an existing identifier such as an RFC822 mailbox) or cn.
tldr.outcome: The memo is Informational, not a standard, and the authors say other approaches are permissible. It has since been updated by RFC 4519.

today: RFC 2377 is an Informational memo, not a standard, and it is updated by RFC 4519. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: The Two-Part Proposal
sections.content:
RFC 2377 describes a directory naming plan as an alternative (or extension) to the conventional X.500 approach. Its authors say the X.500 approach has proven an obstacle to wide deployment of directory-enabled applications on the Internet.

The plan has two main features. First, the root and upper portions of the name hierarchy come from the existing Domain Name System. Second, it offers several options for naming leaf objects such as person objects, including reuse of existing Internet identifiers for people.

Use of the plan is not obligatory. The authors do, however, strongly encourage developers of directory-enabled products, especially LDAP clients and user interfaces, to assume it will see widespread use.
sections.plainLanguage: The plan has two ideas: name the big folders after website-style names that already exist, and name the people inside using labels they already have, like an e-mail address.

sections.title: Why X.500 Naming Struggled
sections.content:
The Internet X.500 Directory Pilot grew to about 1.5 million entries of varying quality, and its growth rate was far lower than that of the Internet. The memo says naming was not the main cause, but it contributed.

The RFC names two problems with the conventional style, where a user's relative distinguished name (RDN) is a cn (common name). First, common names collide among users under the same node, and the fix is an extra attribute that makes the name long and unpopular. Second, X.500 could not reuse many existing names: organization names must be registered, and that can be a difficult and acrimonious process because they are tied to trademarks.

The North American Directory Forum proposed using legal names from the civil naming infrastructure, which led to obscure names such as o="Nadir Networks, Inc.", st=New Jersey, c=US.
sections.plainLanguage: The old way needed everyone to sign up for official, long, unique names, and many people did not bother. Lots of people share a name like Sam Smith, so names alone got mixed up.

sections.title: What a Naming Plan Must Provide
sections.content:
A directory naming plan must give names that are unambiguous within some namespace, at a minimum within one isolated directory server. The RFC lists five further characteristics the plan seeks to satisfy.

  • Hierarchical: permits delegation of name assignment and partitioning of directory information among servers.
  • Friendly to loose coupling of autonomous directory servers. The plan does not try to create a single namespace for all directory objects.
  • Readily usable by LDAP clients and servers.
  • Friendly to reuse of existing Internet name registries such as DNS names and RFC822 mailbox identifiers.
  • Minimally user-friendly: a user should be able to recognize the information encoded in his or her own DN.
sections.plainLanguage: Good names should be unique, easy to sort into groups, work with the tools people already have, borrow existing names, and look familiar to the person they belong to.

sections.title: Constructing Names with dc, uid and cn
sections.content:
Names use three attribute types. The domain component (dc) builds the upper part of a DN from a domain name: an organization with the domain acme.com gets the DN dc=acme, dc=com as the root of its subtree. Subdomains such as corporate.acme.com can name subdivisions, giving dc=corporate, dc=acme, dc=com. The construction algorithm itself is in RFC 2247.

Leaf objects use uid (user identifier) or cn. The plan does not constrain their use. The authors' own practice was uid for person objects where an existing registry of names could be reused, and cn for other objects, for example uid=J.Smith@acme.com, dc=acme, dc=com or cn=Reading Room, dc=physics, dc=national-lab, dc=edu.

The domain name inside a uid value may, but need not, match the dc components. The plan does require that the concatenated domain components form a registered domain name, one that is represented in the DNS, which avoids name conflicts. Applications should not assume a uid is a valid mailbox: the mail attribute should always be checked.
sections.plainLanguage: The big folders are named after a web-style address, like com then acme. Each person inside is labelled with something they already have, like their e-mail address.

sections.title: Directory Schema Changes
sections.content:
Existing X.500 schemas need extending. The plan keeps the usual structural object classes and adds two auxiliary classes: dcObject (defined in RFC 2247) and uidObject, defined here with OID 1.3.6.1.1.3.1, which requires uid. Adding dcObject lets organization and organizationalUnit entries use dc in their RDN.

For people, no extension is needed if inetOrgPerson (preferred) or newPilotPerson is used, though cn stays a required attribute and matters for searching. For servers and server applications the standard schema uses cn; the RFC's SSL example gives the server host.acme.com the DN dc=host, dc=acme, dc=com and a certificate subject of cn=host.acme.com, dc=host, dc=acme, dc=com.

For X.500-style servers the RFC also defines five name forms under the OID branch 1.3.6.1.1.2, such as domainNameForm and uidOrganizationalPersonNameForm.
sections.plainLanguage: The directory's rule book needs a few extra pages so that its entries are allowed to carry these new kinds of labels.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The security section is a single point. Access controls may deny browse access to unauthorized clients on parts of the directory tree. Even so, directory names and the structure of such sensitive portions may be inferable from DNS queries, and giving public visibility to some portions of the tree may help those making such inferences.
sections.plainLanguage: Because the folders are named after public web-style names, someone could guess what is in a hidden part of the directory just by looking at those public names.
